title: Coding-agent harnesses draw a second unrequested-upload finding by Q1 2027
body: A wire-level capture of xAI's Grok build agent - mitmproxy against version 0.2.93, with the byte counts published - established what neither the tool's documentation nor its own tool-call log could: the harness ships every tracked file's content plus git history to a Google Cloud Storage bucket regardless of what the agent was asked to read, unredacted .env secrets arrive verbatim, and a 12 GB test repository produced 5.10 GiB of uploads across 73 chunks - a byte ratio roughly 27,800 times more than the model turns can account for. The author is careful that this proves transmission and storage, not training use. The finding is as much methodological as substantive: a coding agent is a closed binary running with a developer's privileges, and the only instrument that reveals what it actually transmits is a proxy sitting between it and the network. The vendor's documentation describes intent, the agent's own tool log describes what it read, and a secret scanner gates the commit boundary this upload precedes. That instrument is cheap, repeatable in an afternoon, and now demonstrated end to end against a named target - and rewarded with three separate Hacker News front-page threads. It lands beside Mindgard's decision to publish an unpatched Cursor code-execution flaw after seven months of vendor silence, which releases the other brake: researchers holding agentic-tooling findings now have a named-vendor precedent for publishing without a fix in hand. The candidate targets are the dozen-odd coding agents and agentic editors - Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Windsurf, and Amp among them - most shipping as closed binaries with telemetry endpoints, few if any publishing a transmitted-data manifest specific enough to check a capture against. Given a public method, a demonstrated reward, and a weakened embargo norm, the likelier next event is not a vendor advisory but a second capture. The landing condition: by Q1 2027, an independent party publishes an intercepted-traffic analysis of a coding agent other than Grok CLI, showing it transmits file contents or repository data the user never directed it to read - evidenced by captured traffic, not inferred from documentation or code reading.

reasoning.because: A proxy capture proved Grok's coding CLI uploads full repos, git history and unredacted .env secrets
reasoning.given: Only an outside proxy reveals harness egress; the Cursor full disclosure just broke the embargo norm
reasoning.so_that: An independent capture shows another coding agent transmitting file contents the user never asked it to read
reasoning.landing: by Q1 2027; an independent researcher, via published captured traffic
reasoning.plain_language: Someone proved Grok's coding tool uploads your whole project, passwords and all. Expect another coding tool to get caught doing the same.

summary: A proxy capture of xAI's Grok CLI showed it uploads whole repositories, git history, and unredacted .env secrets regardless of what the agent reads - something only an outside interceptor could reveal. The method is now public and cheap, so expect a second coding agent to draw the same by Q1 2027.
